extracted.intended_audience: literate London readership / general readers of The Spectator interested in morals, manners, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A series of short moral and social essays (The Spectator) offering normative rules and examples about personal virtue, charity, conjugal conduct, literary taste, and evaluating public actions (e.g., conquest). Presents tests, examples, and practical advice for behaviour and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests of Good-Nature as a Moral Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules to examine whether good-nature is a true moral virtue rather than a mere constitutional temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First: whether it acts with steadiness and uniformity in sickness and in health, in prosperity and in adversity (transient good-humour is not true philanthropy). Second: whether it operates according to the rules of reason and duty — makes distinctions between deserving and undeserving and does not relieve indiscriminately. Third: whether one is willing to exert it to one's own disadvantage, risking fortune, reputation, health, or ease for the benefit of mankind. Examples and contrasts: Bacon's solicitor (transient selfish timing); Eugenius (generous yet prudent practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity: set aside a proportion and practise prudently
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rule for charitable giving: lay aside a certain proportion of income beyond necessities for the poor, and manage charity so as not to injure one's family or friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose to appropriate a fixed portion (example: Eugenius never values himself above nine-score of his two-hundred pounds, keeping the tenth for charity), make voluntary additions in better years, and use small habitual sacrifices (fasting, walking instead of coach) to increase funds. Redirect entertainment spending (theatre/opera money) to relief when appropriate. Emphasises making gifts without impoverishing oneself or prejudicing family—charity should be generous but prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity as sympathetic, continual practice (examples & motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity should be habitual, modest, and performed in ways that increase the donor's private satisfaction and the recipient's welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative conduct: giving a shilling at end of a walk instead of coach fare; diverting money meant for entertainment to relieve an object met in the street; fasting/abstinence to add to charitable bank. Supported by Scripture (Proverbs; New Testament passages about clothing, feeding, visiting) and literary exempla (Job, epitaph at Doncaster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary balance between wit (Mercurial) and seriousness (Saturnine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should alternate and mix entertaining wit and serious moral reflection to reach both light and thoughtful readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be always grave (lose the gay readers) nor always merry (lose the sober readers). Aim usually to instruct but accept diversion as a means to bring people toward reflection. Use variety so a sprightly reader may be led into profitable thinking and a thoughtful reader may be cheered into mirth. The Spectator's policy: find entertainments of both kinds and, when possible, make mirth instructive and never immoral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid immoral or ill-natured raillery in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: While being diverting, writers must suppress strokes of raillery or ill-nature that tend to corrupt minds or injure reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise discretion: omit witty strokes that have a remote tendency to corrupt readers or glances of ill-nature that could damage another's reputation. The writer may have many thoughts that would please ordinary taste but must modestly blot them for moral reasons (cf. 'Poets lose half the Praise they would have got, Were it but known what they discreetly blot').

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating Conquests: profit measured by subjects, riches, and power vs. costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for judging whether military conquests are beneficial: did they increase the prince's subjects, riches, or power in net terms after accounting for losses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess increase of subjects (use population counts where available), consider economic capacity of acquired provinces, and weigh losses: military casualties (estimates of yearly losses and long-term demographic effects), garrison burdens, famine and depopulation. Example reasoning: compute added inhabitants versus men lost in campaigns and resulting loss of births/household continuity; factor in economic desolation and migration away from war-torn regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal behaviour: husbands' duty to avoid creating domestic torment
rubrics_metrics.description: Husbands ought to behave regularly and agreeably at home and not inflict avoidable anguish (e.g., coldness, absence, treating home like a gaol) that produces jealous suffering in wives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admonish husbands to be more constant and civil in private than they may be in public; avoid leaving home in a manner that makes return feel like entering a gaol; recognise the pain jealousy causes and correct behaviour that needlessly provokes it. The author proposes observing exemplar couples to form a 'System of Conjugal Morality' and to 'admonish Husbands and Wives what Terms they ought to keep towards each other.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for light public amusements (whistling/grinning/yawning contests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for these popular entertainments: whistling judged on clearness and keeping countenance; grinning and yawning judged by naturalness and effect on spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whistling contest: ability to whistle clearest and go through a tune without laughing, despite provocation by a Merry-Andrew; such pastimes improve country music, promote gravity, and teach ordinary people to keep countenance. Yawning contest (Twelfth-Night): widest and most naturally produced yawns that provoke the most yawns in spectators win; these are appropriate seasonal or Bath entertainments and not intended to cause sleep but amusement.
